posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
Sounds like something to try, just remember not to wash the silver nitrate back out of the emulsion.

I seem to be having a little trouble killing the leftover sensitizing dyes in Tmax plates, you may have a similar problem with the litho film. Plain fixing and a carbonate ("dehardener") bath didn't do it and I got substantial fogging, but I did get a thin hologram on my second try. I have a more thoroughly abused plate to try next.

I'm working on it (ever slowly) and will post whatever I figure out, what I tried and how it worked or didn't. I'd be interested to hear of any methods you try and what results you get.

posts.content_md:
I've made some tests with tmax and Ilford film sheet.

Fixing the silver halide out of the film and reload it with the diffusion method. I got some interesting results but don't go farter in the way.

I remember I've trouble to remove the purple stain but after some search, I found this :

[http://www.binbooks.com/books/photo/i/l/5E1B6AF5EB](http://www.binbooks.com/books/photo/i/l/5E1B6AF5EB) (last post)

<....

I have found that using T-F4 fixer completely removes the purple stain

from all Ilford and Kodak B&W films(35mm and 120 formats). T-F4 can be

purchased from Photographers Formulary at:

[http://www.photoformulary.com/](http://www.photoformulary.com/)

Later.....Scott...

....>

Other point. Seems that Tmax and Ilford sheet have their 2 sides coated (probably to avoid curling of the film). Need to remove the second coating (unsilvered) before reload the film. I removed the coating with house bleach.

I've made some tests with those reloaded film and I got holo (very dim) but it works. Maybe a way to make holographic material without the need of coating gelatin (imho the difficultest step of the process)

posts.content_md:
> **jean:** I've made some tests with tmax and Ilford film sheet.Fixing the silver halide out of the film and reload it with the diffusion method. I got some interesting results but don't go farter in the way.(...)I've made some tests with those reloaded film and I got holo (very dim) but it works. Maybe a way to make holographic material without the need of coating gelatin (imho the difficultest step of the process)

Using fixed commercial SH emulsions for the diffusion method might turn out to be a tricky thing. In my opinion the main issue usually is one does not know its previous pretreatment or certain key specifications like grain size. This may differ from one type of commercial emulsion to another. 

Secondly, I have serious doubts that by fixing out the silver halides from a commercial emulsion (and this might particularly apply to larger grains), one will be left with a “virgin” gelatin layer. I don't know what actually happens but it may well be that insoluble by-products remain in the layer. When I tried to reload 8E75 and Ilford SP-673 by means of the diffusion method, I ended up getting very noisy layers (and those grains were in the 30nm range). 

Instead of coating the plates/films oneself one might purchase plates/films from places like: [http://www.filmotec.de/English_Site/Pro ... _40_e.html](http://www.filmotec.de/English_Site/Products/GF_40_e/gf_40_e.html)

By the way DuPont used to sell a gelatin coated Cronar polyester film. Unfortunately, we were never able to find any resellers to deal with small orders...
